claim: A third of adults over the age of 65 suffer from significant hearing loss.
source: A third of adults over the age of 65 suffer from significant hearing loss, a condition exacerbated by two debilitating condition, subjective tinnitus, a phantom ringing or buzzing sensation, and hyperacusis, normal sounds perceived as intolerably loud or even painful.
evidence: This is a general statement about prevalence in the population, likely based on established knowledge or literature.

claim: Roughly 12% of adults experience tinnitus.
source: Roughly 12% of adults experience tinnitus, but the prevalence skyrockets to 50% in young combat personnel (Leske, 1981; Andersson et al., 2002; Cave et al., 2007; Michikawa et al., 2010; Hebert et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The prevalence of tinnitus skyrockets to 50% in young combat personnel.
source: Roughly 12% of adults experience tinnitus, but the prevalence skyrockets to 50% in young combat personnel (Leske, 1981; Andersson et al., 2002; Cave et al., 2007; Michikawa et al., 2010; Hebert et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Tinnitus is costly with more than $2 billion paid annually in veteran disability payments.
source: Tinnitus is costly with more than $2 billion paid annually in veteran disability payments.
evidence: This is a factual statement about economic costs, likely based on established knowledge or reports.

claim: Hyperacusis affects roughly 9% of adults.
source: Hyperacusis affects roughly 9% of adults (Andersson et al., 2002), but its prevalence is likely higher because of the difficulty of self-diagnosis (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The prevalence of hyperacusis is likely higher than 9% because of the difficulty of self-diagnosis.
source: Hyperacusis affects roughly 9% of adults (Andersson et al., 2002), but its prevalence is likely higher because of the difficulty of self-diagnosis (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation and inference from difficulty of diagnosis.

claim: Among those whose primary complaint is hyperacusis, 90% also suffer from tinnitus.
source: Remarkably, among those whose primary complaint is hyperacusis, 90% also suffer from tinnitus (Baguley, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Tinnitus and hyperacusis are often triggered by cochlear hearing loss.
source: Since tinnitus and hyperacusis are often triggered by cochlear hearing loss, it was long assumed that these auditory distortions resulted from hyperactivity disorders in the peripheral auditory nerve.
evidence: This is a statement about the etiology of these conditions, based on established knowledge.

claim: It was long assumed that tinnitus and hyperacusis resulted from hyperactivity disorders in the peripheral auditory nerve.
source: Since tinnitus and hyperacusis are often triggered by cochlear hearing loss, it was long assumed that these auditory distortions resulted from hyperactivity disorders in the peripheral auditory nerve.
evidence: This is a historical statement about prior assumptions in the field.

claim: Auditory nerve spontaneous and sound-evoked firing rates are depressed in subjects with cochlear damage.
source: This hypothesis, however, is contradicted by studies showing that auditory nerve spontaneous and sound-evoked firing rates are depressed in subjects with cochlear damage (Kiang et al., 1970; Wang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Surgical section of the auditory nerve fails to eliminate tinnitus.
source: Moreover, surgical section of the auditory nerve fails to eliminate tinnitus (Baguley et al., 1992; Lockwood et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tinnitus and hyperacusis arise from maladaptive neuroplastic change in the central nervous system provoked by cochlear pathology.
source: These negative results plus recent imaging studies now suggest that tinnitus and hyperacusis arise from maladaptive neuroplastic change in the central nervous system (CNS) provoked by cochlear pathology (Lockwood et al., 1998; Husain et al., 2011; Sereda et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and inference from negative results.

claim: Several models of tinnitus and hyperacusis have been proposed that involve increased central gain, altered functional connectivity, and aberrant neural oscillations in neural networks.
source: Several models of tinnitus and hyperacusis have been proposed that involve increased central gain, altered functional connectivity (FC), and aberrant neural oscillations in neural networks (Weisz et al., 2007; Sereda et al., 2011; Henry et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hyperacusis is associated with enhanced sound-evoked activity in auditory cortex, medial geniculate body, and inferior colliculus.
source: In the context of central gain models, some human imaging data indicate that hyperacusis is associated with enhanced sound-evoked activity in multiple-auditory processing centers, namely auditory cortex (ACx), medial geniculate body (MGB), and inferior colliculus (IC), whereas tinnitus can be triggered solely by enhanced central gain in the ACx (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Tinnitus can be triggered solely by enhanced central gain in the auditory cortex.
source: In the context of central gain models, some human imaging data indicate that hyperacusis is associated with enhanced sound-evoked activity in multiple-auditory processing centers, namely auditory cortex (ACx), medial geniculate body (MGB), and inferior colliculus (IC), whereas tinnitus can be triggered solely by enhanced central gain in the ACx (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Active loudness models suggest that tinnitus arises entirely from increased central noise independent of gain.
source: On the other hand, active loudness models suggest that tinnitus arises entirely from increased central noise independent of gain, whereas hyperacusis results exclusively from increased nonlinear gain that results in loudness intolerance (Zeng, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hyperacusis results exclusively from increased nonlinear gain that results in loudness intolerance.
source: On the other hand, active loudness models suggest that tinnitus arises entirely from increased central noise independent of gain, whereas hyperacusis results exclusively from increased nonlinear gain that results in loudness intolerance (Zeng, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cross-sectional human brain imaging studies have produced diverse, inconsistent, or contradictory findings.
source: While cross-sectional human brain imaging studies have identified many different sites of aberrant neural activity, published results from patients have often produced diverse, inconsistent, or contradictory findings.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Discrepancies in human imaging studies are likely due to confounding factors such as patient heterogeneity, unknown etiology, genetic diversity, social and environmental factors, and duration or severity of tinnitus and hyperacusis.
source: Some discrepancies are likely due to confounding factors such as patient heterogeneity, unknown etiology, genetic diversity, social and environmental factors, and duration or severity of tinnitus and hyperacusis.
evidence: This is an inference about the causes of discrepancies in the literature.

claim: Animal models could potentially overcome many limitations of human studies provided that tinnitus and hyperacusis can be reliably induced, behaviorally measured, and functionally imaged.
source: Animal models could potentially overcome many of these limitations provided that tinnitus and hyperacusis can be reliably induced, behaviorally measured, and functionally imaged.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential of animal models.

claim: The percentage of individuals developing tinnitus after intense noise exposure is highly variable and its duration is unpredictable.
source: While tinnitus can develop in some individuals after intense noise exposure, the percentage of affected individuals is highly variable and its duration is unpredictable (Heffner and Harrington, 2002; Lobarinas et al., 2006; Heffner, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High doses of aspirin have long been known to consistently induce acute tinnitus in humans and animals.
source: High doses of aspirin, an anti-inflammatory drug used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, have long been known to consistently induce acute tinnitus in humans and animals (Myers and Bernstein, 1965; Myers et al., 1965; Mongan et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-dose sodium salicylate consistently induces tinnitus.
source: Moreover, high-dose sodium salicylate (SS), the active ingredient in aspirin, not only consistently induces tinnitus (Jastreboff et al., 1988; Lobarinas et al., 2004; Stolzberg et al., 2013), but also hyperacusis (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2014); these perceptual disorders disappear a day or two post-treatment.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-dose sodium salicylate induces hyperacusis.
source: Moreover, high-dose sodium salicylate (SS), the active ingredient in aspirin, not only consistently induces tinnitus (Jastreboff et al., 1988; Lobarinas et al., 2004; Stolzberg et al., 2013), but also hyperacusis (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2014); these perceptual disorders disappear a day or two post-treatment.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SS-induced tinnitus and hyperacusis disappear a day or two post-treatment.
source: Moreover, high-dose sodium salicylate (SS), the active ingredient in aspirin, not only consistently induces tinnitus (Jastreboff et al., 1988; Lobarinas et al., 2004; Stolzberg et al., 2013), but also hyperacusis (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2014); these perceptual disorders disappear a day or two post-treatment.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All three rats tested developed tinnitus-like behavior after SS treatment.
source: All three rats developed tinnitus-like behavior; data from two representative animals are shown in Figure 1A,B.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: During baseline testing, rats correctly identified Quiet trials at greater than 70% correct and AM and NBN trials at greater than 80% correct.
source: During baseline testing (B1–B4; B6–B9), rats correctly identified Quiet (no sound stimulus) trials at greater than 70% correct and AM and NBN trials >80% correct.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Saline-control treatment had no noticeable effect on performance during Quiet, NBN, or AM trials.
source: The saline-control treatment had no noticeable effect on performance during Quiet, NBN, or AM trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: When rats were treated with SS, performance dropped to 50% or less only on Quiet trials.
source: However, when the rats were treated with SS, performance dropped to 50% or less only on Quiet trials, that is, rats shifted their response preference from the feeder associated with Quiet to the feeder associated with a continuous NBN, behavior indicative of tinnitus.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Rats shifted their response preference from the feeder associated with Quiet to the feeder associated with a continuous NBN after SS treatment, behavior indicative of tinnitus.
source: However, when the rats were treated with SS, performance dropped to 50% or less only on Quiet trials, that is, rats shifted their response preference from the feeder associated with Quiet to the feeder associated with a continuous NBN, behavior indicative of tinnitus.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results and interpretation.

claim: When SS treatment was discontinued, performance on Quiet trials returned to baseline indicating that tinnitus had disappeared.
source: When SS treatment was discontinued (P1–P4), performance on Quiet trials returned to baseline indicating that tinnitus had disappeared.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results and interpretation.

claim: Performance on NBN and AM trials was unaffected by SS treatment indicating that behavior was under sound stimulus control.
source: Performance on NBN and AM trials was unaffected indicating that behavior was under sound stimulus control.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results and interpretation.

claim: Reaction time–intensity functions obtained with Saline were nearly identical to those obtained during baseline.
source: Reaction time–time intensity functions obtained with Saline were nearly identical to those obtained during baseline indicating that the injection had no effect on behavior.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Reaction times obtained after SS were significantly different from baseline at low and high intensities.
source: In contrast, reaction times obtained after SS were significantly different from baseline at low and high intensities [Two-way, repeated measures ANOVA; significant effect of treatment (p < 0.0001), intensity(p < 0.0001), interaction of treatment × sound intensity (p < 0.001); Bonferroni post-hoc analysis between baseline and SS significant at 30 dB (p < 0.001), 50 dB (p < 0.05), 60 dB (p < 0.01), 70 and 80 dB (p < 0.001), and 90 dB (p < 0.05)].
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with statistical analysis.

claim: Reaction times after SS were significantly shorter than baseline at moderate to high intensities, behavioral evidence indicative of hyperacusis.
source: Reaction times after SS were significantly shorter than baseline at moderate to high intensities behavioral evidence indicative of hyperacusis, that is, these intensities were perceived as louder than normal (Lauer and Dooling, 2007; Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results, interpretation, and citation support.

claim: At 30 dB SPL reaction times were longer than normal due to hearing loss, which reduces the loudness of sounds near threshold.
source: However, at 30 dB SPL (sound pressure level) reaction times were longer than normal due to hearing loss, which reduces the loudness of sounds near threshold.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results and interpretation.

claim: Reaction time–intensity functions returned to normal after SS treatment was discontinued.
source: Reaction time–intensity functions returned to normal after SS treatment was discontinued (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: SS treatment caused a significant increase in startle amplitude at 95 and 105 dB SPL.
source: SS treatment caused a significant increase in startle amplitude at 95 and 105 dB SPL [Two-way, repeated measure, ANOVA, significant main effect of intensity (p < 0.001), treatment (p < 0.001), intensity × treatment interaction (p < 0.001); Bonferroni post-test significant at 95 dB and 105 dB (p < 0.001)].
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with statistical analysis.

claim: Startle amplitudes returned to normal when SS was discontinued.
source: Startle amplitudes returned to normal when SS was discontinued (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: SS is known to cause temporary hearing loss and reduce the neural output of the cochlea.
source: SS is known to cause temporary hearing loss and reduce the neural output of the cochlea.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge.

claim: The mean CAP amplitude-intensity function measured 2 hr after SS treatment was shifted to the right at low intensities due to a threshold shift of approximately 20 dB.
source: The mean (+SEM) CAP amplitude-intensity function (average of 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 30, and 40 kHz) measured 2 hr after SS treatment was shifted to the right at low intensities due to a threshold shift of approximately 20 dB (horizontal arrow, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to a figure.

claim: The amplitude of the CAP was greatly reduced (70–80%) at suprathreshold intensities after SS treatment.
source: In addition, the amplitude of the CAP was greatly reduced (70–80%) at suprathreshold intensities (down arrow, Figure 2A) indicating a profound reduction in the neural output of the cochlea.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to a figure and interpretation.

claim: LFP amplitude-intensity functions from the MGB, ACx, and LA were shifted to the right approximately 20 dB 2 hr post-SS.
source: The LFP amplitude-intensity functions from all three structures were shifted to the right approximately 20 dB (Figure 2B–D) 2 hr post-SS consistent with the CAP.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures.

claim: The threshold shift measured in central structures is largely determined by the loss of sensitivity at the cochlea.
source: These results indicate that the threshold shift measured in central structures is largely determined by the loss of sensitivity at the cochlea.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: LFP amplitudes in the MGB, ACx, and LA became substantially larger than pre-treatment values after SS treatment.
source: LFP amplitudes in the MGB, ACx, and LA increased rapidly with increasing intensity, and response amplitudes became substantially larger than pre-treatment values (Figure 2B–D) in contrast to the large CAP amplitude reductions (∼70% decrease) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures.

claim: The SS-induced enhancement of suprathreshold LFP amplitudes at 100 dB SPL was approximately 50% in the MGB and 140% in the ACx.
source: The SS-induced enhancement of suprathreshold LFP amplitudes at 100 dB SPL was approximately 50% in the MGB and 140% in the ACx, results indicative of a progressive increase in gain from peripheral to more central auditory loci (Noreña, 2010; Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with interpretation and citation support.

claim: SS produced significant bilateral increases in ALFF in the parafloccular lobes (PFL, 38–37 voxels) and cerebellar lobules 4 (CB4, 38–37 voxels).
source: Within the cerebellum, SS produced significant bilateral increases in ALFF in the parafloccular lobes (PFL, 38–37 voxels) and cerebellar lobules 4 (CB4, 38–37 voxels) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures and table.

claim: Significant bilateral increases in ALFF were observed in the gigantocellular reticular nucleus/oral region of the pontine reticular nucleus (RN/PnO, 35–28 voxels) after SS treatment.
source: Significant bilateral increases in ALFF were also observed in subcortical areas that included the gigantocellular reticular nucleus/oral region of the pontine reticular nucleus (RN/PnO, 35–28 voxels, Figure 3C) and pontine reticular nucleus/paramedian raphe nucleus (PnO/PMr, 12–10 voxels, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures.

claim: Significant bilateral increases in ALFF occurred in the inferior colliculus (IC, 72–68 voxels) after SS treatment.
source: In the midbrain, significant bilateral increases in ALFF occurred in the IC, a binaural auditory processing area (IC, 72–68 voxels, Figure 3C,D) (Skaliora et al., 2004) and superior colliculus (SC, 40–43 voxels, Figure 3D), a visual center with multisensory inputs (Wallace et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures and citations.

claim: Significant bilateral increases in ALFF occurred in the superior colliculus (SC, 40–43 voxels) after SS treatment.
source: In the midbrain, significant bilateral increases in ALFF occurred in the IC, a binaural auditory processing area (IC, 72–68 voxels, Figure 3C,D) (Skaliora et al., 2004) and superior colliculus (SC, 40–43 voxels, Figure 3D), a visual center with multisensory inputs (Wallace et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures and citations.

claim: Significant bilateral increases in ALFF occurred in the medial geniculate body (MGB, 52–48 voxels) after SS treatment.
source: Significant bilateral increases also occurred in the MGB (MGB, 52–48 voxels), a high-level auditory processing area (Figure 3E–G), in the ACx (ACx, 167–178 voxels, Figure 3E–H), visual cortex (VCx, 32–39 voxels, Figure 3C,D), somatosensory cortex (SSCx, 37–40 voxels, Figure 3I–K), and amygdala (AMY, 61–60 voxels, Figure 3E–H).

claim: Significant bilateral increases in ALFF occurred in the amygdala (AMY, 61–60 voxels) after SS treatment.

source: As shown in Figure 4 and Table 2 (cluster size, t-values shown for left and right hemispheres), when the seed region was in the ACx, there were significant bilateral increases of FC in large clusters located in the MGB (62–70 voxels), IC (82–88 voxels), and AMY (67–68 voxels) plus moderate clusters located in the RN (52–48 voxels), PFL (39–35 voxels), and CB4 (51–53 voxels).

claim: When the seed region was in the ACx, there were significant bilateral increases of FC in the RN (52–48 voxels), PFL (39–35 voxels), and CB4 (51–53 voxels).
source: As shown in Figure 4 and Table 2 (cluster size, t-values shown for left and right hemispheres), when the seed region was in the ACx, there were significant bilateral increases of FC in large clusters located in the MGB (62–70 voxels), IC (82–88 voxels), and AMY (67–68 voxels) plus moderate clusters located in the RN (52–48 voxels), PFL (39–35 voxels), and CB4 (51–53 voxels).

claim: No decreases in FC were observed when the seed region was in the ACx.

claim: No decreases in FC were seen when the seed regions were located in MGB.

claim: SS induced a peripheral threshold shift of approximately 20 dB for the CAP.
source: SS induced a peripheral threshold shift of approximately 20 dB for the CAP (Figure 2A) (Chen et al., 2013, 2014).

claim: The same amount of threshold shift occurred at higher levels of the auditory pathway indicating that the SS-induced hearing loss originates in the cochlea and is relayed centrally.
source: The same amount of threshold shift occurred at higher levels of the auditory pathway indicating that the SS-induced hearing loss originates in the cochlea and is relayed centrally.

source: SS also reduced the CAP neural output by ∼70% at suprathreshold intensities.

claim: Suprathreshold LFP amplitudes in the MGB, ACx, and LA were larger than normal despite the massive reduction in the output of the cochlea.
source: Paradoxically, suprathreshold LFP amplitudes in the MGB, ACx, and LA were larger than normal despite the massive reduction in the output of the cochlea (Figure 2B–D).

claim: These findings provide compelling evidence for an increase in central gain, a form of homeostatic plasticity implicated in tinnitus and hyperacusis.
source: These provocative findings provide compelling evidence for an increase in central gain, a form of homeostatic plasticity implicated in tinnitus and hyperacusis (Salvi et al., 1990; Auerbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with citation support.

claim: The enhanced LFPs seen in ACx are consistent with the enhanced fMRI response observed in the ACx of tinnitus patients.
source: The enhanced LFPs seen in ACx are consistent with the enhanced fMRI response observed in the ACx of tinnitus patients, whereas the enhanced LFPs seen in both ACx and MGB are consistent with the enhanced fMRI responses observed these regions in hyperacusis patients (Gu et al., 2010).

claim: The enhanced LFPs seen in both ACx and MGB are consistent with the enhanced fMRI responses observed in these regions in hyperacusis patients.

evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Hyperacusis was initially observed at 50 dB SPL, the same low intensity at which sound-evoked neural hyperactivity occurred in the ACx.
source: Behaviorally, hyperacusis was initially observed at 50 dB SPL; the same low intensity at which sound-evoked neural hyperactivity occurred in the ACx.

claim: Sound-evoked hyperactivity occurred at noticeably higher intensities for the LA (∼60 dB SPL), MGB (∼70 dB SPL), and acoustic-startle reflex amplitude (∼95 dB SPL).
source: In contrast, sound-evoked hyperactivity occurred at noticeably higher intensities for the LA (∼60 dB SPL), MGB (∼70 dB SPL), and acoustic-startle reflex amplitude (∼95 dB SPL).

claim: Neural responses from the ACx may be one of the most sensitive biomarkers of hyperacusis.
source: These results suggest that neural responses from the ACx may be one of the most sensitive biomarkers of hyperacusis (Juckel et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with citation support.

claim: Loudness intolerance issues likely result from multiple stages of neural amplification as signals are relayed rostrally from the cochlea to the ACx.
source: However, since neural responses increased in magnitude from cochlea to cortex, loudness intolerance issues likely result from multiple stages of neural amplification as signals are relayed rostrally from the cochlea to the ACx (Auerbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with citation support.

claim: SS either decreased or had no effect on spontaneous spike rate in primary ACx.
source: SS either decreased or had no effect on spontaneous spike rate in primary ACx (Ochi and Eggermont, 1996; Yang et al., 2007) and reportedly no effect on synchrony between neuron pairs (Eggermont, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: SS had no effect on synchrony between neuron pairs in primary ACx.
source: SS either decreased or had no effect on spontaneous spike rate in primary ACx (Ochi and Eggermont, 1996; Yang et al., 2007) and reportedly no effect on synchrony between neuron pairs (Eggermont, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The increase in very low-frequency BOLD oscillations (0.01 Hz) represented by ALFF could be interpreted as evidence for increased presynaptic synchrony.
source: However, the increase in very low-frequency BOLD oscillations (0.01 Hz) represented by ALFF could be interpreted as evidence for increased presynaptic synchrony, which would likely enhance spike synchrony albeit at much longer time intervals than previously studied or over much larger neuronal populations than that reflected by spike correlations between neuron pairs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: SS has been found to increase gamma-band (50–100 Hz) oscillatory activity in ACx.
source: SS has also been found to increase gamma-band (50–100 Hz) oscillatory activity in ACx (Stolzberg et al., 2013); oscillations substantially higher than in ALFF.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The tinnitus percept is derived from coordinated activity among several auditory and nonauditory regions.
source: An alternative view is that the tinnitus percept is derived from coordinated activity among several auditory and nonauditory regions (Horwitz and Braun, 2004; Husain et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Enhanced FC between the HIP and auditory areas provides a substrate for assigning a spatial location to a phantom sound.
source: Enhanced FC between the HIP and auditory areas provides a substrate for assigning a spatial location to a phantom sound, while coordinated activity between specific auditory areas and the reticular formation and AMY may draw attention to and add emotional significance to neural activity in the auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Coordinated activity between specific auditory areas and the reticular formation and AMY may draw attention to and add emotional significance to neural activity in the auditory pathway.
source: Enhanced FC between the HIP and auditory areas provides a substrate for assigning a spatial location to a phantom sound, while coordinated activity between specific auditory areas and the reticular formation and AMY may draw attention to and add emotional significance to neural activity in the auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Functionally coordinated activity within the network may be essential for bringing tinnitus into consciousness.
source: Thus, functionally coordinated activity within the network may be essential for bringing tinnitus into consciousness.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: SS increased ALFF and FC in a broad-neural network that included core auditory structures extending from the IC to the ACx.
source: In the resting state, SS increased ALFF and FC in a broad-neural network that included core auditory structures extending from the IC to the ACx consistent with previous studies implicating these central auditory structures in tinnitus (Paul et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with citation support.

claim: The cerebellum is mainly involved in motor planning and control.
source: Although the cerebellum is mainly involved in motor planning and control, some cerebellar regions such as the PFL and vermis receive inputs from auditory centers (Petacchi et al., 2005) and respond to sound (Lockwood et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Some cerebellar regions such as the PFL and vermis receive inputs from auditory centers and respond to sound.
source: Although the cerebellum is mainly involved in motor planning and control, some cerebellar regions such as the PFL and vermis receive inputs from auditory centers (Petacchi et al., 2005) and respond to sound (Lockwood et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The perception of tinnitus has been linked to activation of the PFL and vermis.
source: Interestingly, the perception of tinnitus has been linked to activation of the PFL and vermis (Brozoski et al., 2007a) consistent with our results.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Ablation or inactivation of the PFL eliminates the perception of noise-induced tinnitus.
source: Since ablation or inactivation of the PFL eliminates the perception of noise-induced tinnitus (Bauer et al., 2013), some have suggested that the PFL acts as a gain control mechanism comparing the afferent input from the cochlea with descending signals from the ACx (Bauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The PFL acts as a gain control mechanism comparing the afferent input from the cochlea with descending signals from the ACx.
source: Since ablation or inactivation of the PFL eliminates the perception of noise-induced tinnitus (Bauer et al., 2013), some have suggested that the PFL acts as a gain control mechanism comparing the afferent input from the cochlea with descending signals from the ACx (Bauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: SS leads to hyperactivity in the ACx and increases the FC between the ACx and PFL and CB4.
source: Consistent with this view, our results show that SS leads to hyperactivity in the ACx and increases the FC between the ACx and PFL and CB4.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: If the cerebellar-tinnitus gating hypothesis is correct, then ablating or inactivating the PFL should suppress behavioral measures of SS-induced tinnitus and possibly hyperacusis.
source: If this cerebellar-tinnitus gating hypothesis is correct, then ablating or inactivating the PFL should suppress behavioral measures of SS-induced tinnitus and possibly hyperacusis, providing a clear test of this model.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: The AMY assigns emotions such as fear or anxiety to sensory events.
source: The AMY, which assigns emotions such as fear or anxiety to sensory events, lies outside the classical auditory pathway; however, it is linked to several auditory areas and responds robustly to sound (Romanski and LeDoux, 1993; Stutzmann et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The AMY is linked to several auditory areas and responds robustly to sound.
source: The AMY, which assigns emotions such as fear or anxiety to sensory events, lies outside the classical auditory pathway; however, it is linked to several auditory areas and responds robustly to sound (Romanski and LeDoux, 1993; Stutzmann et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: SS enhanced the ALFF in the AMY and increased FC between ACx and AMY.
source: In the resting state, SS enhanced the ALFF in the AMY and increased FC between ACx and AMY consistent with prior results showing increased coupling between ACx and AMY in tinnitus patients (Kim et al., 2012) and increased c-fos immunolabeling in the AMY following SS treatment (Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with citation support.

claim: SS enhanced sound-evoked activity in the AMY consistent with the increased activation seen in the AMY of hyperacusis patients.
source: SS also enhanced sound-evoked activity in the AMY consistent with the increased activation seen in the AMY of hyperacusis patients (Levitin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with citation support.

claim: Infusion of SS directly into AMY increases sound-evoked activity in the ACx.
source: Importantly, infusion of SS directly into AMY increases sound-evoked activity in the ACx, effects that illustrate the potent independent role that the AMY can exert on central auditory function and aural perception (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The AMY contributes to the fear and anxiety experienced by many patients with tinnitus and hyperacusis.
source: Collectively, these results reinforce the view that the AMY contributes to the fear and anxiety experienced by many patients with tinnitus and hyperacusis (van Veen et al., 1998; Juris et al., 2013; Aazh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with citation support.

claim: Sound and cognitive therapies aimed at reducing the emotional distress of tinnitus and hyperacusis would be expected to reduce the level of activity in the AMY and/or the functional coupling between the AMY and ACx without necessarily eliminating aberrant auditory percepts.
source: Sound and cognitive therapies aimed at reducing the emotional distress of tinnitus and hyperacusis would be expected to reduce the level of activity in the AMY and/or the functional coupling between the AMY and ACx without necessarily eliminating aberrant auditory percepts (Hazell and Jastreboff, 1990).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the experimental results and prior research, supported by citation.

claim: SS-induced enhancement of ALFF in the reticular formation (RN, PnO, and PMr) together with increased FC between the reticular formation and ACx is a novel finding.
source: A novel finding observed during resting-state fMRI was the SS-induced enhancement of ALFF in the reticular formation (RN, PnO, and PMr) together with increased FC between the reticular formation and ACx.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: The reticular formation is an important arousal center with numerous inputs from the cochlear nucleus and IC.
source: The reticular formation is an important arousal center with numerous inputs from the cochlear nucleus and IC (Kandler and Herbert, 1991).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Giant neurons in pontine reticular formation control the amplitude of the acoustic startle reflex.
source: Giant neurons in pontine reticular formation control the amplitude of the acoustic startle reflex (Koch et al., 1992), and stimulation of the AMY enhances the response of these giant neurons (Koch et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Stimulation of the AMY enhances the response of giant neurons in pontine reticular formation.
source: Giant neurons in pontine reticular formation control the amplitude of the acoustic startle reflex (Koch et al., 1992), and stimulation of the AMY enhances the response of these giant neurons (Koch et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The SS-induced increases of ALFF observed in the AMY and reticular formation likely contribute to the enhancement of the acoustic startle reflex.
source: Thus, the SS-induced increases of ALFF observed in the AMY and reticular formation likely contribute to the enhancement of the acoustic startle reflex.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: SS unexpectedly increased ALFF in SSCx, VCx, and SC.
source: SS unexpectedly increased ALFF in SSCx, VCx, and SC raising the question of whether this might be linked to phantom visual or somatosensory perceptions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Heightened ALFF activity in ACx, MGB, and IC could spill over and enhance activity in visual and somatosensory areas.
source: One possibility is that heightened ALFF activity in ACx, MGB, and IC could spill over and enhance activity in visual and somatosensory areas (Murray et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results with citation support.

claim: The SS-induced cochlear loss could unmask pre-existing multisensory circuits in visual and somatosensory areas leading to increased activation.
source: Alternatively, the SS-induced cochlear loss could unmask pre-existing multisensory circuits in visual and somatosensory areas leading to increased activation (Barone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results with citation support.

claim: SS has long been known to cause tinnitus.
source: Although SS has long been known to cause tinnitus (Mongan et al., 1973; Jastreboff et al., 1988), it is now clear that it also induces strong hyperacusis-like behavior (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and prior research, supported by citations.

claim: SS induces strong hyperacusis-like behavior.
source: Although SS has long been known to cause tinnitus (Mongan et al., 1973; Jastreboff et al., 1988), it is now clear that it also induces strong hyperacusis-like behavior (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Tinnitus and hyperacusis frequently co-occur more frequently than previously believed.
source: Although tinnitus and hyperacusis could conceivably arise from different mechanisms (Zeng, 2013), they frequently co-occur more frequently than previously believed (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Tinnitus and hyperacusis are linked to other brain regions associated with emotions, arousal, memories, spatial location, and motor activity.
source: Tinnitus and hyperacusis do not exist in isolation but are linked to other brain regions associated with emotions, arousal, memories, spatial location, and motor activity as schematized in the tinnitus–hyperacusis network model defined by our imaging results (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figure.

claim: With the seed region in IC, a significant increase in FC occurred in the MGB, likely due to the SS-induced enhancement of ALFF in the IC, which is relayed rostrally to the MGB.
source: With the seed region in IC, a significant increase in FC occurred in the MGB; this increase is likely due to the SS-induced enhancement of ALFF in the IC, which is relayed rostrally to the MGB (Figure 5, thick black line) resulting in a larger and more coherent MGB response.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with reference to figure.

claim: With the seed in the MGB, increased FC occurred in the ACx, likely due to the increased ALFF and FC occurring in MGB, which is relayed rostrally to the ACx.
source: Similarly, with the seed in the MGB, increased FC occurred in the ACx; this increase is likely due to the increased ALFF and FC occurring in MGB, which is relayed rostrally to the ACx (Figure 5, thick black line).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with reference to figure.

claim: With the seed in the ACx, increased FC was seen in the MGB and IC, raising the possibility of a recurrent feedback loop in this auditory subnetwork.
source: With the seed in the ACx, increased FC was seen in the same two lower auditory centers, the MGB and IC, raising the possibility of a recurrent feedback loop in this auditory subnetwork (Figure 5, shaded area, bidirectional dashed red lines).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with reference to figure.

claim: SS enhances the FC and response magnitude in a central auditory subnetwork that extends from the IC through the MGB to the ACx.
source: These data combined with our electrophysiological results suggest that SS enhances the FC and response magnitude in a central auditory subnetwork that extends from the IC through the MGB to the ACx.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The ACx is a major hub in the tinnitus–hyperacusis network with side branches that extend caudally to the AMY, RN, and cerebellum (PFL, CB4).
source: The FC data suggest that the ACx is a major hub in the tinnitus–hyperacusis network with side branches that extend caudally to the AMY, RN, and cerebellum (PFL, CB4); these subdivisions all show large SS-induced increases in ALFF, as well as increased FC with the ACx.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The side branch connecting the ACx to the AMY provides a pathway through which emotional significance can be attached to tinnitus or hyperacusis.
source: The side branch connecting the ACx to the AMY provides a pathway through which emotional significance can be attached to tinnitus or hyperacusis (Chen et al., 2014) consistent with earlier studies linking anxiety, annoyance, and fear to tinnitus and hyperacusis (Moller, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results with citation support.

claim: The ACx-RN network provides a conduit by which increased arousal can increase awareness or attention, enhance motivation, or amplify motor responses to tinnitus or suprathreshold sounds.
source: The ACx-RN network provides a conduit by which increased arousal can increase awareness or attention, enhance motivation, or amplify motor responses to tinnitus or suprathreshold sounds (Carlson and Willott, 1998; Paus, 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results with citation support.

claim: The ACx-cerebellar branch could serve as a gating path for tinnitus or modulate the motor responses to or perceptual salience of suprathreshold sounds thereby contributing to hyperacusis.
source: The ACx-cerebellar branch could serve as a gating path for tinnitus (Boyen et al., 2014) or modulate the motor responses to or perceptual salience of suprathreshold sounds thereby contributing to hyperacusis (Mobbs et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results with citation support.

claim: Increased FC between HIP-MGB and HIP-IC could facilitate the formation or stabilization of a memory trace for tinnitus, assign a spatial location to the phantom sound within or outside the head, or promote the retrieval of previously stored auditory memories.
source: Increased FC between HIP-MGB and HIP-IC could facilitate the formation or stabilization of a memory trace for tinnitus, assign a spatial location to the phantom sound within or outside the head, or promote the retrieval of previously stored auditory memories (De Ridder et al., 2006; Ulanovsky and Moss, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results with citation support.

claim: High-dose SS is one of the most predictable and reliable inducers of tinnitus and hyperacusis.
source: Since high-dose SS is one of the most predictable and reliable inducers of tinnitus and hyperacusis, SS provides researchers with a powerful tool to gain mechanistic insights into the neurophysiological conditions needed to induce these debilitating auditory perceptions.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Some of the neuro-pathophysiological changes observed with SS are likely to be similar to those that occur during the early stages of tinnitus or hyperacusis induced by acoustic trauma, Meniere's disease, or sudden hearing loss.
source: Since SS-induced tinnitus and hyperacusis are transient phenomena that begin shortly after drug treatment, some of the neuro-pathophysiological changes we observed are likely to be similar to those that occur during the early stages of tinnitus or hyperacusis induced by acoustic trauma, Meniere's disease, or sudden hearing loss.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the experimental results.

claim: Most individuals develop transient tinnitus immediately post-exposure to acoustic overstimulation, which gradually disappears; only a small percentage develops permanent tinnitus.
source: In cases of acoustic overstimulation, most individuals develop transient tinnitus immediately post-exposure, which gradually disappears; interestingly only a small percentage develops permanent tinnitus (Gilles et al., 2012; Degeest et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: An important question that remains to be answered is whether the neural correlates of chronic tinnitus and hyperacusis are similar or different from the immediate and acute condition.
source: Thus, an important question that remains to be answered is whether the neural correlates of chronic tinnitus and hyperacusis are similar or different from the immediate and acute condition.
evidence: This is a statement about an open research question.

source: SS-induced tinnitus and hyperacusis appear to arise from enhanced central gain and increased FC in an auditory network with four side branches.

source: The core of the network is composed of auditory structures extending from the IC, through the MGB to the ACx plus branches to the AMY, RN, cerebellum, and HIP.
